caveat: Outlook is an analytical assessment as of October 2026, not a forecast. 2025 figures are IMF estimates/projections.
data_source: IMF World Economic Outlook via DataMapper (latest vintage, accessed October 2026)
debt_management: Denmark's public debt is among Europe's lowest: 33.2% of GDP in 2006, a peak of 50% in 2011 after the financial-crisis interventions, then a steady decline to a projected 27.5% in 2025, the series low (45.2% in 2020, 33.3% in 2022). GDP grew from $283.4bn in 2006 to a projected $461.7bn in 2025. Conservative fiscal rules, budget surpluses in good years, and growth have combined to make debt a non-issue; the policy debate is about how to spend the fiscal space, not sustainability.
inflation_management: The krone's peg to the euro obliges the Nationalbank to shadow ECB policy, which it did faithfully: inflation was 1.1% in 2009, 0.3% in 2020, then 8.6% in 2022, the series high, on the energy shock — closely tracking the euro area. It fell to 1.3% in 2024 and is projected at 1.8% for 2025, back near target. The peg has never come under serious pressure during this period; Denmark's reserve buffers and credibility make the shadow rate effective. Notably, Danish mortgage markets absorbed negative rates in the 2010s without systemic damage.

key_events.event: Global financial crisis and a domestic housing bust; debt peaked at 50% of GDP in 2011.
Negative interest-rate era: the Nationalbank defended the euro peg through deep negative rates.
COVID-19: debt rose to 45.2% of GDP; swift fiscal response contained the damage.
Energy shock pushed inflation to 8.6%, tracked by Danish rate hikes shadowing the ECB.
Debt projected at 27.5% of GDP, the series low, on continued surpluses.

outlook_next_decade: Denmark's outlook is one of the strongest in Europe: minimal debt, credible institutions, and a diversified economy with a leading green-energy sector. The fiscal challenge is intergenerational — using space wisely on climate and aging rather than solvency. Inflation should track the ECB target via the peg. The main exposure is external: a small open economy highly sensitive to global trade and the energy transition's pace.
